Patrick Kenehan Archambault Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Research Division I think, obviously, the execution looked great, and -- but my one question would be just can you help us walk a little bit from -- I think, your margin is adjusted 10% x ZEV credits. It sounds like you still have some levers to pull to get to the 25%. Can you just go through those with us? Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer Well, I think -- Patrick, it's Deepak here. Our automotive gross margin, excluding ZEV credits, is closer to 13%, and maybe we could walk you through that later on to clarify. I know this is a confusing quarter with significant accounting numbers here, so we'll just help you with that. But we see clearly a path that gets us to 25%, excluding ZEV credits, given the actions that are underway and have been underway for a while. And these relate to -- on the cost-reduction aspects with our part cost-reduction roadmap, the efficiencies we have in our manufacturing and supply chain that are happening over the second half, as well as a combination of the new options that we have put in the marketplace and the margin enhancement we get from there. I'm sure Elon has more to add. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Right. Well -- I mean, just in summary, I mean, we're about 12 points away from getting to the 25% gross margin target without ZEV credits. And if you look at, say, Q1 to Q2, we increased 8 points. So obviously, on average, between Q3 and Q4, we need to do 6 points per quarter, so we need maybe not to make as quite as big as an improvement as we did Q1 to Q2, but obviously, still a significant hill to climb and huge amount of work. But we feel pretty confident about the 25% number, and it's important that there's -- we have visibility into these numbers within reason ahead of time. So the things that affect the gross margin -- in order for them to affect the fourth quarter, we really need to be in place or substantially in place about a month before the fourth quarter. Otherwise, the parts that go into the car will not contain the cost savings that are necessary. So essentially, things need to be in place next month. And so that's not very far away. So that's why we feel -- felt confident enough to reaffirm the 25% gross margin guidance, absent ZEV credits for the fourth quarter. There could be a force majeure event or something, some really big unexpected thing, but as long as there's nothing really unusual that happens, then that should meet that target. Patrick Kenehan Archambault Goldman Sachs Group Inc., Research Division Okay, great. And then I guess I haven't -- we haven't had an update on the X and when that's likely to -- we understand that, obviously, the variance of the S or what's taking a lot of engineering resources kind of in the near term. Deepak, maybe in terms of the X timing, is it still towards the end of next year when you're thinking about it? And when do those engineering resources sort of come to bear on your capital budget? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect So I'll maybe do part of the answer and then hand it over to Deepak. But we're hard at work on the Model X, refining the design. We expect to be in limited -- with a small number of units at the end of next year, and then volume production would only occur in 2015. So in terms of -- if you're trying to sort of model it financially, I'd model it more in 2015 than 2014, although we're on track to deliver units to the customers TESLA, INC. Operator Our next question comes from Andrea James with Dougherty & Company. Andrea Susan James Dougherty & Company LLC, Research Division I guess I imagine you have several options available to you now. I mean, from investing in the Model S capacity, which you mentioned in your letter, to finishing up the Model X and then to engineering the next- generation vehicle. And I was wondering if you could just weigh your priorities and tell us how you're thinking about it, both from factory investment and also from your R&D. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Okay. Well, the -- okay, so it depend on how you -- how one weighs those things. So in terms of our expenditures, we're still more on Model S than anything else on every front, including R&D. Because bear in mind, we've got a right-hand drive that's coming out in the spring and then there's the China version. And obviously, we got the European version that's going in there. There are number of nuances in the various European countries that require work to ensure the car operates smoothly. There's the Japan right-hand drive version. So there's a lot of versions and, individually, maybe not so huge, but you add them up and they amount to CapEx spending. In terms of executive time, I think we're -- the Model X is swiftly rising to become the main priority. It's not quite there yet, but it will be soon. I'm allocating an increasing portion of my time to that every week. Probably in the fourth quarter, it becomes the top one, the top item, is my guess. These are somewhat qualitative statements, but -- yes. Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer Yes. In the capital expenditure for Model S, it will primarily kick in next year as we start to get some of the tooling phase. Right now, it's about more of the human resource expenditure and some of the... Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect It's like the design and engineering, but not a lot of tooling. So it's a lot of lab work and design work, but not a lot of hard-tooling or anything. Yes, there'll be fairly big chunk of that in the second and third quarter and fourth quarter next year. Andrea Susan James Dougherty & Company LLC, Research Division When does the next generation of vehicle sort of move up? Is it a timing thing? Is it a -- is it a cost of the battery pack thing that resources... Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect TESLA, INC. But when you do the math on saying, okay, how many batteries do you need for -- like what's the cell fabrication capability, the raw materials, all the elements, it's -- there's -- so it's really quite a large number in order to ultimately say, feed a factory that's producing 0.5 million vehicles a year. Adam Michael Jonas Morgan Stanley, Research Division Okay, Elon, I'm not going to ask you any questions about a cap raise this time. I don't think we need to go there. First question, on the 40,000 unit annualized sales comment you made by late 2014 as a potential, what metric were you using when you were extrapolating that for Asia? Is that something like on a sales per store or percentage of addressable market? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Actually, it's just based on what we kind of see the demand as. Like -- I mean, right now, obviously, we're selling in North America at about 20,000 units a year. So Europe is a similar-sized market to North America. China is actually bigger, and then that doesn't include the rest of Asia Pacific, South America, South Africa, Australia. And so again -- I mean -- so it seems like that's a pretty safe number to assume. I don't think we probably got some potential upside from that number. Adam Michael Jonas Morgan Stanley, Research Division Okay, that's clear. Just next one, can you elaborate a bit on the nature of the supplier bottlenecks that you mentioned? Is it related to homologation for some of the exotic, either European or right-hand drive type deliveries? Is it a new issue or is it -- was it a lingering legacy issue? Any update on when this could be resolved? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. This is an important point. But our production -- we're production constraint, not demand constraint. Very often, I mean, -- people will suggest all sorts of marketing ideas and this, that and the other thing. But obviously, our time is spent trying to figure out how to make more cars. And the things that prevent us from doing that are supplier parts, essentially. And we've got -- like 90% of our suppliers are able to ramp up and 5% have some difficulty and 4% have a lot of difficulty and 1% just can't. And so we've got to replace those or in-source those items, because you -- you can't supply -- give people a car that's 99% complete, unfortunately, and there are several thousand unique parts in the car. So that's where we're really spending our time on is clearing up those production bottlenecks or supply chain bottlenecks. And I think we should have probably cleared most of them out in the next 6 months. I think by the end of Q1, Q2, we should -- sort of like Q2, I think, unlock a fair bit more production potential. Then we'll see what the demand looks like at that point. But we're striving to become demand limited as opposed to production limited. And I feel like we're actually able to attract kind of more the A-Team on suppliers. Whereas previously, we had some trouble attracting A-Team from suppliers, because they thought we wouldn't be around long term. And we have that issue where IHS had predicted that Tesla would only ever sell 3,000 cars lifetime of the Model S, and then we sold that in the first -- basically, the first quarter of production. And so the tricky thing was that a lot of us -- many of our supplies had taken IHS number or taken like historical electric vehicle numbers and maybe given us a little bit of credit for our projections, but not much. And so they didn't tool up for the production that we actually experienced as we were scrambling to make up for it. And yes, so that's really -- they just didn't believe it. So it takes some time to tool up and do it. And then some suppliers, a small number, they're just not set-up for volume production, so we've got to switch them out or in-source it. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Well, I'm glad to see that BMW is bringing electric car to market. That's cool. For Deepak, the first question, ask you to bridge on gross margin through the end of the year. Could you just maybe give us, on the bridge of improvement from 1Q to 2Q, the big chunks of things that contributed to that margin increase x ZEV credits? Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer Sure. I would say that the biggest pieces there were part cost reduction as we continue to get more efficient in -- at our suppliers, as well as some of the design changes to be made to make the design efficient while not taking anything away from a consumer point of view. We also had improvements in our labor and overhead and our freight costs. And all of those, in fact, were partially offset by the mix. We had a poor mix in Q2 since we sold the 40-kilowatt-hour cars that had the 60-kilowatt-hour battery pack... Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect And we essentially sold at loss, I think. Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer Right, right. Yes, which had, from a average gross margin perspective, a negative impact. So I think what I'm sharing with you is no different than what we have shared before. It's those same levers and part cost is our biggest lever that helps to drive these improvements. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. The parts, labor and -- yes, parts and labor. That's what cars are made of. The -- yes. And I think -- maybe another way to characterize it is like in the fourth quarter of last year, we were extremely dumb at making cars. In the first quarter, we were maybe still pretty dumb, and we're slightly dumb in the second quarter. And hopefully, by the fourth quarter, we will, at least, not be dumb. I think that actually -- if you think about it. Brian Arthur Johnson Barclays Bank PLC, Research Division I'll figure out how to quantify that. TESLA, INC. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect This is not some super -- how did we get so super good. It's like how do we stop being so stupid. Brian Arthur Johnson Barclays Bank PLC, Research Division Second question, Gen3, the 32 questions underneath. The $35,000 price point, is that before or after regulatory -- excuse me, consumer credits and tax credits? And then second, as you kind of think of Gen3 and making money at it, some talk I've heard that maybe small-format batteries aren't the right way to go, but large format, just maybe reiterate. I'd kind of think the former, small format, kind of where you are on those and how that gives you some comfort in getting to the price point on the Gen3. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Sure. So the $35,000 does not assume -- assumes that the $7,500 federal tax credit is no longer available, and there may be other sort of state level tax credit, so maybe other things. But we're assuming that the $35,000 is the -- is without any subsidy. It's always helpful to have some subsidy, but we're not counting on it. And yes, so in terms of the cell format. For us, when we talk to our key cell suppliers and we ask them to give us -- say, at the sale level, what is the best energy density, so brought us pure down and what is the best price sort of dollars per watt hour. Invariably, the 18650 format is the best by -- usually by a pretty decent margin, and that's an 18 millimeter by 65 millimeter cylinder with -- yes. Yes, that's the format that seems to be the best. It has advantages. I think -- you could say why is it -- does it cost less, I mean, I think you're able to kind of pack and then why does it have that engine if you're able to compress and pack in quite a bit of electrode and electrolyte in that cylinder. That's why batteries really were like conservative batteries are -- things like cylinder or AA, AAA and that kind of thing. So you can pack more in there. And this just happens to be a fairly efficient manufacturing process in almost every way relative to the sort of prismatic approach. Also, as you make the cell bigger, you have to say that the reject rate for the cell is going to increase. So if you think of maybe an analogy to the silicon wafer fab and say, what would be cheaper, having a whole bunch of, say, 6-inch wafers or one 12-inch wafer. And actually it's the lower diameter wafer that is cheaper, because with silicon, as with electrode area, you have to reject anything that's got a flow. So the reject rate -- and this also help us think things inner limit. So, say, inner limit, where the battery -- where the whole battery is one cell, the reject rate will be virtually 100% or -- and then as you make the cell smaller and smaller, the reject rate will reduce. And at the 18650 format, reject rates stay low and very good statistical reliability. So I'm sort of giving long- winded answers here but... Brian Arthur Johnson Barclays Bank PLC, Research Division Shorthand, could we call it a server rack versus a mainframe strategy? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes, sure. Brian Arthur Johnson Barclays Bank PLC, Research Division Okay. And in terms of how you're managing the load, are there advantages to having several thousand, I've heard numbers of 5,000 to 8,000 cells versus a smaller number? Again, kind of thinking about the statistics behind it. Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect TESLA, INC. FQ2 2013 EARNINGS CALL | AUG 07, 2013 Copyright © 2019 S&P Global Market Intelligence, a division of S&P Global Inc. All Rights reserved. spglobal.com/marketintelligence 11 Well, I think we're at around 7,000 cell number for the 85-kilowatt-hour pack. If we were to -- what's the ideal cell number and if we were to do a whole new cell, like a whole new sort of cell plant, I mean, I think we might drop the cell number in half, but probably not less than that. And another thing that cells give you is that for long-term life of the pack, if you have a large number of cells, then losing a cell actually has a very small impact on the total capacity of a pack. Whereas if you have a small number of cells, then losing a cell has a big impact on the -- yes, on the capacity of the pack. So there are some advantages for life as well and for reliability. So maybe that's why we're not going to, say, assume it's just going to be good as North America. But it's -- yes, it's probably at least half as good as North America, and maybe it is, ultimately, as good as North America. But our conservative estimate, we'll say, is half as good. And then China and rest of Asia and other countries, well, if they could be half as good as North America, then we're at the 40,000 unit number, and that -- so that all seems pretty reasonable to me... Daniel V. Galves Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division That makes sense. In terms of capacity to build, I think your current line is set up for maybe 40,000 units to 50,000 units on 2 shifts. And what is the decision making process in terms of potentially adding more capacity if you're going to fill that up with just the Model S? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Right. And yes -- and as I said earlier, while we have the ability to produce at the 40,000-unit level, all of our suppliers must also have that ability. So that's the thing that's holding us back. I think we -- there's a TESLA, INC. FQ2 2013 EARNINGS CALL | AUG 07, 2013 Copyright © 2019 S&P Global Market Intelligence, a division of S&P Global Inc. You mentioned that the changes to options and pricing that went in maybe a week ago was going to be a benefit to margin in the back half.
